# Megaliths, Leys, and the Deep Archives

## The standing circles

> status: ratified (D-0029, D-0180)

The author's own extension of the extended-mind principle: stones arranged into a
Stonehenge-like circle are a sort of supercomputer — reasoning infrastructure at
landscape scale. What a scrap of vellum does for one mind and a loom does for a
village, a standing circle does for a region: it holds arguments too vast for any
gathering of humans to carry unaided. They are the oldest built things in the world,
older than the current cycle's kingdoms, and they were built to be public.
In the approved single-system architecture, a circle is regional-scale premise and
argument infrastructure. It localizes, stores, times, and distributes proof; it is not
a separate stone-magic.

## How the circles are used and misused

> status: provisional (D-0072)

The session's working model: interfacing with a circle is positional and calendrical —
where you stand, when you speak. The old cultures used the circles to balance
season-scale reciprocity. The empire, unable to build such things, encloses them:
walls a circle inside a keep and forces it to hold the ledger's fictions. A circle
made to carry lies runs hot — the surrounding land shows it (blackened chalk, stillborn
lambs, copper-tasting springwater), and the common folk read those signs long before
any scribe admits fault.

## Leys and bogs

> status: provisional (D-0072)

Between circles run old alignments — leys — along which the land itself seems to pass
consequence faster than a walker could carry news. And beneath everything, the bogs:
anaerobic, patient, preserving. What the empire burns, the bog keeps — cloth, bodies,
carved wood, whole outlawed testimonies sunk deliberately by the persecuted as deep
storage for a better century. Bog-recovery is dangerous, sacred work, and the
far-future orders build their archives in bogs for exactly this reason ([[religion]],
[[cycles]]).

## The broken network

> status: provisional (D-0072)

The empire's centuries of stone-breaking ([[breaking-of-the-stones]]) did not merely
censor the past; it fractured the
land's capacity to balance itself at scale, leaving isolated pockets where local
proofs still hold and long corridors where nothing does. Whether anything
continent-scale can ever be rebuilt — or whether the future is deliberately,
permanently local — is one of the story's live questions.

## Surface discipline

> status: ratified (D-0030)

All of the above is written and heard as pure animist fantasy: stones, alignments,
bogs, memory. The computational allegory is for the authors' room only. No character
reaches for a modern metaphor, ever (see `data/banned-vocabulary.yaml`).
